nodes.label: 'Ma moj!' Slang Retort (ungrammatical affirmative of nemoj)
nodes.rationale: The source explicitly flags this as slang: there is no grammatical affirmative counterpart to the negative imperative nemoj, but B, C, and S colloquial usage has produced the ungrammatical-yet-popular retort 'Ma moj!'/'Ma da moj!' in response to 'Ma nemoj!', compared by the authors to English 'No way!' → 'Way!' — the project's first source-explicitly-labeled slang item.
nodes.community_name: Flagship Textbook: Cases, Dialect Tags & Early Slang
nodes.norm_label: 'ma moj!' slang retort (ungrammatical affirmative of nemoj)

nodes.label: [B]/[C]/[S] Dialect-Tag Convention
nodes.rationale: The book's own boxed note (Lesson 2, p.23) explains letters after a word signal either (a) a pan-BCS word with a regionally restricted alternate, or (b) two competing words with different varieties preferring different ones. Lesson 6's grammar note further explains Montenegrin is deliberately NOT given a fourth [M] tag because its 2007 codification was too recent/unvalidated at time of writing. Lesson 5 warns a [C]/[S] tag does not always mean strict binary exclusivity — some tagged words simply coexist with a pan-regional [B,C,S] synonym.
nodes.community_name: Flagship Textbook: Cases, Dialect Tags & Early Slang
nodes.norm_label: [b]/[c]/[s] dialect-tag convention

nodes.label: Genitive Case (formation and uses)
nodes.rationale: Introduced in Lesson 4: masc./neut. Gsg endings equal the animate accusative; feminine takes -e (a-stem) or -i (consonant-stem). Governs prepositions like iz, kod, od, bez, do, blizu, and the invariant nema. Genitive plural (Lesson 5) has two endings, -a (default) and -i (consonant-stem feminines plus mesec/mjesec, ljudi, sat), required after numbers 5+ and adverbs of measure.
nodes.community_name: Flagship Textbook: Cases, Dialect Tags & Early Slang
nodes.norm_label: genitive case (formation and uses)

nodes.label: Locative/Dative/Instrumental Case System
nodes.rationale: Locative (Lesson 6) appears only after prepositions (na/u for location vs accusative for motion — the 'u-words'/'na-words' distinction, memorized per noun). Dative (Lesson 6) shares singular forms with locative and marks indirect objects plus dative-experiencer state constructions (dosadno mu je). Instrumental (Lesson 7) marks means/manner, time of repeated action, and governs prepositions s/sa, pred, nad, za. In the plural (Lesson 8) all three cases merge into one form per noun (-ama for fem. -a nouns, -ima elsewhere).
nodes.community_name: Flagship Textbook: Cases, Dialect Tags & Early Slang
nodes.norm_label: locative/dative/instrumental case system

nodes.label: Clitic Word-Order Rule
nodes.rationale: Clitics (li, auxiliary forms of biti, dative/genitive-accusative object pronouns, se, and the 3sg auxiliary je) must occupy a strict slot order and sit in the clause's second position. Lesson 6 gives the basic order LI–aux–dat–acc/gen–SE–JE; Lesson 10 refines this with the 'je-final' rule where the 3sg auxiliary alone moves to the end.
nodes.community_name: Flagship Textbook: Cases, Dialect Tags & Early Slang
nodes.norm_label: clitic word-order rule

nodes.label: Comparative/Superlative Adjective Formation
nodes.rationale: Comparative degree is marked by suffix -ij- (with naj- prefixed for superlative) for most adjectives, by consonant-softening of the stem-final consonant for a productive second class (kràtak→kraći), or by suppletion for four common adjectives (dobar/bolji, loš/gori, velik/veći, mali/manji). Adverbs are built from the neuter singular comparative/superlative form, with divergent meanings for više ('taller' adj / 'more' adv) and manje ('smaller' adj / 'less' adv).
nodes.community_name: Flagship Textbook: Cases, Dialect Tags & Early Slang
nodes.norm_label: comparative/superlative adjective formation

nodes.rationale: Colloquial interjections and filler/tag particles documented with explicit regional attribution: bona/bolan (Bosnian, term of address like 'man'), bre (Serbian emphasis filler, like 'you know'), je li?/jel'?/jel'da?/jel'te? (interrogative tags, contracted forms used by some Croatian/Bosnian speakers), ovaj (word-groping filler), jao/joj (exclamations).

nodes.label: Ekavian/Ijekavian ([E]/[J]) Pronunciation Split
nodes.rationale: Where Common Slavic jat historically stood, Croatian/Bosnian reflect it as ije (long jat) or je (short jat, 'ijekavian'), Serbian reflects it as e ('ekavian') in most of Serbia proper, but ijekavian in Bosnia, southwestern Serbia, and Montenegro — so this split cuts across the B/C/S national-standard split rather than mapping one-to-one onto it (documented explicitly in Lesson 3's dialect note).
nodes.community_name: Flagship Textbook: Cases, Dialect Tags & Early Slang
nodes.norm_label: ekavian/ijekavian ([e]/[j]) pronunciation split

nodes.label: BCS Future Tense (clitic hoću-auxiliary)
nodes.rationale: A compound tense: infinitive (or da+present) plus a clitic/full auxiliary derived from hteti/htjeti 'to want' (ću, ćeš, će...). Word-order/spelling of the fused clitic differs by standard: Croatian keeps -t and writes separately (učit ću), Serbian drops -t and fuses (učiću); Bosnian permits both. The clitic auxiliary and 'want'-meaning full forms are genuinely homophonous, disambiguated by context or by substituting željeti/željeti for unambiguous 'want.'
nodes.community_name: Flagship Textbook: Cases, Dialect Tags & Early Slang
nodes.norm_label: bcs future tense (clitic hocu-auxiliary)

nodes.label: Negation and the Double-Negative Requirement
nodes.rationale: The particle ne fused before a verb negates the sentence; ni- prefixed to interrogatives forms negative pronouns (niko/nitko 'nobody', ništa 'nothing') that grammatically require the verb to ALSO be negated (nè vidim nikoga), a required double negative rather than emphasis. Negated prepositional phrases split the two-part negative pronoun around the preposition (ni o čemu). The particle zar opens yes/no questions expecting a negative answer or expressing surprise.
nodes.community_name: Flagship Textbook: Cases, Dialect Tags & Early Slang
nodes.norm_label: negation and the double-negative requirement

nodes.label: Passive Participle Formation
nodes.rationale: Formed with one of three markers (-n, -t, -en) attached to the infinitive or present stem depending on conjugation type, sometimes requiring the same consonant-softening set used in comparatives, verbal nouns, and the feminine instrumental singular (k→č, g→ž, h→š, t→ć, d→đ, etc.).
nodes.community_name: Flagship Textbook: Cases, Dialect Tags & Early Slang
nodes.norm_label: passive participle formation

nodes.label: Past Tense (biti + L-participle)
nodes.rationale: Periphrastic past tense: present tense of biti (clitic, normally) plus an L-participle agreeing with the subject in gender/number. Lesson 10 details formation across all 16 verb conjugation types and the 'je-final' clitic-ordering rule when the 3sg auxiliary je is adjacent to se or the feminine accusative clitic je (which becomes ju).
nodes.community_name: Flagship Textbook: Cases, Dialect Tags & Early Slang
nodes.norm_label: past tense (biti + l-participle)

nodes.label: The Particle se (Reflexive/Passive/Reciprocal/Inclinational)
nodes.rationale: Se marks true reflexive (umiti se 'wash one's face'), impersonal (tamo se dobro jede), inclinational/desire (ide mi se, nè ide mi se), intransitive, non-causative (budim se vs majka me budi), passive, and reciprocal (čuti se 'be in touch by phone', vole se) functions. Some verbs never occur without se (bojati se, nalaziti se).
nodes.community_name: Flagship Textbook: Cases, Dialect Tags & Early Slang
nodes.norm_label: the particle se (reflexive/passive/reciprocal/inclinational)

nodes.label: Regional/Teen Colloquial Family Terms
nodes.rationale: Lesson 9's cultural note documents a rich set of regionally-restricted colloquial father/mother terms — babo/nana (parts of Bosnia), ćaća/papo (Dalmatia), japa (Zagorje near Zagreb), ćale (Belgrade) — plus Belgrade slang keva 'Mom' (explicitly labeled slang by the source) and a pan-regional teenage register: stara/stari/starci ('old woman'/'old man'/'oldsters', addressing mother/father/parents). Flagged by the extraction checklist as the first source-self-labeled slang finds in the project alongside Lesson 7's 'Ma moj!'.

nodes.label: 'Slavic' vs. 'Slovenian' Cross-Dialect Ambiguity Trap
nodes.rationale: 'Slavic' is slavenski in Croatian, slovenski in Serbian/Bosnian; but 'Slovenian' is slovenski in Croatian and slovenački in Serbian — i.e. the Croatian word for 'Slovenian' is identical in form to the Serbian/Bosnian word for 'Slavic', a genuine cross-dialect false-friend the source flags explicitly and which Bosnian usage resolves by publication-date convention (post-1990 texts favor the Croatian spelling).
nodes.community_name: Flagship Textbook: Cases, Dialect Tags & Early Slang
nodes.norm_label: 'slavic' vs. 'slovenian' cross-dialect ambiguity trap

nodes.label: Subjectless Dative/Accusative Experiencer Constructions
nodes.rationale: Sentences with no grammatical subject, or a 'logical subject' in a non-nominative case: dative (sviđati se 'to like', dosadno mu je 'he's bored'), genitive (mnogo ih ima), accusative (strah me je 'I'm afraid' — experiencer of an emotion). Always take 3sg present / neuter singular L-participle in the past.
nodes.community_name: Flagship Textbook: Cases, Dialect Tags & Early Slang
nodes.norm_label: subjectless dative/accusative experiencer constructions

nodes.label: Verbal Aspect (Perfective/Imperfective)
nodes.rationale: Most verbal ideas have two corresponding verbs sharing a root but differing in aspect: perfective for a single completed action, imperfective for repeated/ongoing/general action (e.g. kupiti P vs kupovati I, both 'to buy'). Aspect pairs form by prefixation (adds closure, e.g. jesti→pojesti) or suffixation (changes conjugation type, e.g. davati/dati). Motion-verb pairs keep the same prefix but change root (otići vs odlaziti).
nodes.community_name: Flagship Textbook: Cases, Dialect Tags & Early Slang
nodes.norm_label: verbal aspect (perfective/imperfective)

nodes.label: Three-Way 'Take/Carry' Root Distinction (nos-/vod-/voz-)
nodes.rationale: BCS distinguishes three near-rhyming imperfective roots for 'take/carry [somewhere]' by what is moved: nositi (inanimate object or a carried being, e.g. infant), voditi (a being moving under its own power on foot), voziti (moved by vehicle). Perfectives exist only prefixed, using distinct roots -nes-/-ved-/-vez- (most neutrally with prefix od-).
nodes.community_name: Flagship Textbook: Cases, Dialect Tags & Early Slang
nodes.norm_label: three-way 'take/carry' root distinction (nos-/vod-/voz-)

nodes.label: Sociolinguistic Rationale: Montenegrin Excluded as a Fourth [M] Tag
nodes.rationale: The source explicitly declines to add an [M] tag: Montenegro's 2006 independence and 2007 constitution named 'Montenegrin' the official language and set up a 2008 codification council, but as of the book's writing that process was too recent/unvalidated by the speech community; unlike B/C/S (whose separateness the source partly ties to distinct religious/cultural histories), Montenegro is described as sharing that cultural history with Serbia. Directly explains why this whole extraction only tracks [B]/[C]/[S], not a fourth tag.

nodes.label: Bosnian Turkish-Derived Kinship Vocabulary
nodes.rationale: Bosnian retains a set of Turkish-derived kinship words reflecting Islamic cultural heritage that stand apart from the shared B/C/S terms: amidža 'paternal uncle' (vs. stric [B,C,S]), dajdža 'maternal uncle' (vs. ujak [B,C,S]), nena 'grandmother' (vs. baba/baka [S,C]). A parallel Bošnjak/Bosanac ethnonym-vs-demonym distinction (Muslim community member vs. any B&H resident regardless of ethnicity) is flagged as sociolinguistically significant in Lesson 1.
nodes.community_name: Lesson 1 Variants & Bosnian Turkish Kinship Terms
nodes.norm_label: bosnian turkish-derived kinship vocabulary

nodes.label: BCS Fusional Morphological Typology
nodes.rationale: Grammatical categories (case, number, gender) are merged into single, non-separable affixes rather than agglutinated as distinct stacked morphemes. Held across the full-book bridge-scale extraction (Lessons 1-20 plus appendices/glossary, ~8,450 rows) — no agglutinative or polysynthetic behavior turned up anywhere, so no morpheme breakdowns are needed in any output file for this language.
